row.basis: unknown owner; restore the animal
row.note: The verse anticipates finding a straying animal when its owner is not near or is not known, keeping it until the owner seeks it, and restoring it; this is a close legal counterpart to the dālla camel whose rab/mālik is unknown.

row.basis: straying ox or sheep
row.note: The command to return a brother’s ox or sheep that has gone astray gives the commentary’s escaped animal a concrete action and owner relation rather than treating “straying” as an abstraction.

row.basis: enemy’s wandering ox or donkey
row.note: Even an enemy’s wandering ox or donkey must be returned; the scene joins a loose pack animal to the obligation created by its known owner.

row.basis: when a roadside animal counts as lost
row.note: The mishnah distinguishes an animal merely grazing on a road from one whose state shows genuine loss, then requires return; it gives a legal test for the commentary’s concrete dālla rather than equating every free animal with a lost one.

row.basis: identifying signs for restitution
row.note: The discussion of simanim in the law of lost property makes an identifying sign the means by which an item can be restored; it is a direct legal analogue to the camel’s wasm/sīmah by which it is recognized.

row.basis: speckled and spotted flock as wages
row.note: Jacob sets visibly marked sheep and goats apart as his wages, so an animal’s visible feature allocates it within a flock to a particular claimant.

row.basis: visible color proving ownership or theft
row.note: Jacob says the flock’s visible coloring will demonstrate his innocence and expose a stolen animal; this makes an animal mark an evidentiary sign of whose it is.

row.basis: ox knows owner; donkey master’s manger
row.note: Isaiah says an ox knows its owner and a donkey its master’s manger while Israel does not know; it directly parallels the commentary’s claim that livestock recognize owner and place while humans can be more lost.

row.basis: lost sheep; misleading shepherds; resting place
row.note: Jeremiah calls the people lost sheep, says their shepherds led them astray, and says they forgot their resting place; it combines the commentary’s stray animal, failed leader, path, and merabb-like place of remaining.

row.basis: lost sheep asks to be sought
row.note: The speaker says that he has gone astray like a lost sheep and asks the Lord to seek his servant, turning the lost-animal image into a prayer for recovery by the rightful master.

row.basis: seek the lost and bring back the strayed
row.note: God’s shepherding promise explicitly seeks the lost and returns the strayed, supplying the caring owner-side of the commentary’s camel left in an unowned place.

row.basis: Moses follows a runaway lamb to water
row.note: The midrash has Moses pursue a lamb that has run from Jethro’s flock, find it drinking, and carry it back; God makes that care the reason he can shepherd Israel, joining the stray animal, water/pasture, and qualified leader.

row.basis: one lost sheep sought by its owner
row.note: The man who loses one of a hundred sheep goes after the lost one, a direct recovery scene for the commentary’s animal separated from its owner and herd.

row.basis: one strayed sheep valued above the ninety-nine
row.note: This lost-sheep version has the shepherd seek the one that strayed and value it above the ninety-nine, a distinct Christian apocryphal intensification of the individual animal’s recovery.

row.basis: straying sheep return to Shepherd and Overseer
row.note: The addressees were sheep going astray but have returned to a Shepherd and Overseer; it connects wandering from the way with restoration to a guiding, responsible figure.

row.basis: own sheep called by name and led out
row.note: The shepherd calls his own sheep by name and leads them out, joining recognized belonging with a leader who initiates the flock’s movement.

row.basis: shepherd goes ahead and sheep follow
row.note: The shepherd goes in front and the sheep follow his voice, the closest New Testament rendering of the commentary’s front animal/hādī followed by the rest of the herd.

row.basis: owner and flock know one another
row.note: The reciprocal knowledge of shepherd and sheep gives a direct positive counterpart to the dālla whose rab and mālik cannot be identified.

row.basis: sheep without a shepherd
row.note: Jesus sees the crowds as sheep without a shepherd; the image makes the lack of a leading, responsible figure the cause of a dispersed and distressed flock.

row.basis: leader goes out before the people
row.note: Moses asks for a leader who will go out before and bring the people in, so that they will not be sheep without a shepherd; it applies the commentary’s front-leading herd image to communal guidance.

row.basis: God goes before to lead by the way
row.note: The Lord goes before Israel in the pillar to lead them on the way, giving the request for guidance a concrete leading-before movement like the commentary’s hādī.

row.basis: what goes ahead seeks a resting place
row.note: The ark goes before the people to seek out a resting place for them; it binds the front guide to finding the place where the moving community may remain.

row.basis: people led like sheep through wilderness
row.note: God leads the people out like sheep and guides them like a flock in the wilderness, directly joining flock, guidance, and a journey through exposed country.

row.basis: YHWH as shepherd
row.note: The declaration that the Lord is the speaker’s shepherd gives the commentary’s rab/mālik relation its classic pastoral form: a flock has a guiding provider.

row.basis: green pastures and resting waters
row.note: The shepherd makes the sheep lie in green pastures and leads them to resting waters, closely matching the herd’s fixed place and the pasture it finds pleasing.

row.basis: leading in right tracks
row.note: The shepherd restores life and leads in right tracks, providing a pastoral analogue to ihdinā and the straight path rather than guidance as a disembodied instruction.

row.basis: shepherd feeds, gathers, and gently leads
row.note: The divine shepherd feeds the flock, gathers lambs, and gently leads nursing ewes; it develops both pasture-care and differentiated leadership within a herd.

row.basis: good pasture and secure lying down
row.note: God promises good pasture where the flock will lie down, a precise counterpart to the merabb where camels stay and the land whose grazing is approved.

row.basis: Wisdom guides on straight paths
row.note: Wisdom guides the righteous person on straight paths in its account of divine guidance; it supplies a Jewish Second Temple formulation for the commentary’s moving sense of the straight path.

row.basis: unknown paths made straight
row.note: God leads the blind on an unknown way and makes crooked ground straight, directly pairing guidance with the contrast between a right path and a deviating one.

row.basis: perverting the straight paths of the Lord
row.note: The rebuke names the straight paths of the Lord and accuses its target of making them crooked, a concrete New Testament counterpart to the commentary’s path that turns aside from the qasd.

row.basis: forsaking the straight way and going astray
row.note: The text says its opponents abandoned the straight way and went astray, retaining both sides of the commentary’s road vocabulary rather than merely a general moral failure.

row.basis: Lamb shepherds and guides to springs
row.note: The Lamb becomes the flock’s shepherd and guides them to springs of water; this striking reversal makes an animal the leader while retaining the commentary’s guide-and-pasture movement.

row.basis: followers go wherever the Lamb goes
row.note: The redeemed follow the Lamb wherever he goes, an explicit following relation that gives the commentary’s herd behind its leading animal a Christian eschatological form.

row.basis: all cattle belong to God
row.note: God declares every forest beast and the cattle on a thousand hills to be his, a direct biblical counterpart to the commentary’s claim that every creature has its rab/mālik.

row.basis: divine blessing includes six thousand camels
row.note: The verse calls Job’s latter state blessed and immediately counts his camels among its abundance, closely matching the commentary’s association of camels with niʿma, benefit, and blessing.

row.basis: camels bear precious cargo over distance
row.note: A multitude of camels carries gold and frankincense and brings proclamation of the Lord’s praises; it closely matches the commentary’s load-bearing animals and its hamd/benefit frame.

row.basis: grass grown for cattle
row.note: God causes grass to grow for cattle, giving the good pasture in the commentary a providential source rather than treating it as only a herd preference.

row.basis: donkey lying under its burden
row.note: The command to help an enemy’s donkey collapsed under its load gives an ethical counterpart to the commentary’s carrying mount: its legs bear burdens, so the human associated with it must assist.

row.basis: human rule over living creatures
row.note: Humanity is told to rule the moving creatures, a creation-account counterpart to the commentary’s Qur’anic picture of livestock made subject to human possession; the biblical verse frames that relation as a commission.

row.basis: the righteous know an animal’s needs
row.note: The righteous person knows the life or needs of his animal, adding responsibility and attention to the commentary’s owner-and-herd relation.

row.basis: divine pity includes much cattle
row.note: God’s stated pity for Nineveh explicitly includes its many cattle, a concrete biblical companion to the commentary’s move from useful animals to the Lord’s compassion.

row.basis: wild ass sent free and unbound
row.note: Job asks who released the wild ass and loosed its bonds; it gives the commentary’s wild-ass herd a theological counterweight to the tame, owner-marked animal.

row.basis: wild ass given wilderness as home
row.note: God gives the wild ass the steppe and salt land as its dwelling, making the wilderness place in the commentary’s lost-animal definition a positive habitat for a creature not domesticated by humans.

row.basis: horse and mule need bit and bridle
row.note: The psalm contrasts a human who should understand with horse and mule controlled by bridle; its training image usefully complicates the commentary’s tame camel and animal-led guidance without making the two moral claims identical.

row.basis: name written on the forehead
row.note: The Lamb’s followers visibly bear his and his Father’s name on their foreheads, a personal and covenantal analogue to the commentary’s visible brand that makes an animal’s belonging recognizable.

row.basis: bees ordered under a king
row.note: Basil’s bee discussion presents the hive as an ordered community under a king; it supplies a Christian natural-theological analogue to the commentary’s malik of the bees, though section divisions vary by edition.

row.basis: unmuzzled ox re-read for human workers
row.note: Paul invokes the rule against muzzling a grain-treading ox in an argument about the support of human workers; this Christian reading turns a working animal’s claim into a claim about labor, relevant to the commentary’s tamed, load-bearing animal.

row.basis: Hebrew melek goes before the people
row.note: Hebrew melek is cognate with the commentary’s m-l-k label, and this verse asks for a king who will go before Israel; its own context thus pairs the cognate title with the front-leading function the commentary gives to milk.

row.basis: Hebrew ʿbd, serving YHWH
row.note: Hebrew ʿbd is cognate with the commentary’s Arabic ʿ-b-d label; Joshua’s choice to serve the Lord supplies the worship-side use of that family, without transferring the camel-treatment sense into the verse.

row.basis: Hebrew noʿam and paths
row.note: Hebrew noʿam is cognate with the commentary’s n-ʿ-m label, and Wisdom’s ways are called ways of pleasantness; the verse joins the source’s blessing/pleasant-pasture association to a path.

row.basis: Aramaic Rabbi as an authority title
row.note: The source labels rabb as an owner-title; John retains the Semitic title Rabbi and glosses it as Teacher. The likely cognate relation supplies only a title comparison here, not evidence that John’s teacher image is a flock-owner image.

row.basis: Lord’s mercy trains and turns back like a shepherd
row.note: Sirach describes the Lord’s compassion as rebuking, training, teaching, and turning creatures back as a shepherd turns his flock; it gathers the commentary’s merciful rab, tamed animal, straying, and restoration into one Jewish formulation.

row.basis: donkey turns aside because it sees the angel
row.note: Balaam’s donkey leaves the road after seeing the divine messenger while its human rider cannot see and beats it. The scene reverses the surface value of an animal’s turning aside: the animal is the one properly guided, sharpening the commentary’s animal-and-human contrast.

row.basis: trained heifer; fair neck; harness
row.note: Hosea calls Ephraim a trained heifer and describes placing a yoke on its fair neck for work; this is a close prophetic animal image for the commentary’s muʿabbad camel and its guiding neck.

row.basis: cords of love; yoke lifted; feeding
row.note: God leads Israel with cords of kindness and love, lifts the yoke from its jaws, and bends down to feed it. The verse combines animal training, gentle leading, pasture-like provision, and divine compassion.

row.basis: wild ox will not serve or stay at the manger
row.note: The divine questions ask whether the wild ox will consent to serve a human or spend the night at the manger, directly contrasting a human-owned, tamed herd with a wild bovine beyond ordinary possession.

row.basis: wild ox bound to furrow and harrow
row.note: The next question tests whether the wild ox can be bound with a cord to plow and harrow; it supplies the laboring, guided-animal side of the commentary’s mount carried and directed by its body.

row.basis: camel humps carrying treasure through hard country
row.note: The oracle pictures wealth carried on camels’ humps through a land of distress, a specific Hebrew Bible counterpart to the commentary’s animals carrying burdens to distant places.

row.basis: where the shepherd pastures and lets flock rest
row.note: The beloved asks where the shepherd pastures his flock and makes it lie down at noon, directly matching the commentary’s owner, grazing place, and place of remaining.

row.basis: follow flock tracks and pasture kids near shepherd tents
row.note: The reply directs the seeker to go out by the tracks of the flock and pasture her kids beside shepherds’ tents; it gives an unusually exact literary image of following a herd’s route toward a shepherded grazing place.

row.basis: led by water on a straight path without stumbling
row.note: God promises to lead the returning people by streams of water on a straight way where they will not stumble, binding the commentary’s guidance request, straight path, and animal-water/pasture scene.

row.basis: compassionate guide leads to water springs
row.note: The compassionate one leads the hungry and thirsty and guides them by springs of water, a direct guide-and-pasture counterpart to the hādī leading a herd.

row.basis: flock wanders for lack of shepherd
row.note: The people wander like sheep and suffer because there is no shepherd, making the absence of the commentary’s front-leading, responsible figure the stated cause of dispersion.

row.basis: know the condition of flocks and attend to herds
row.note: The proverb requires careful knowledge of the state of one’s flock and attention to herds, adding the sustained ownerly care absent from the unknown-owner definition of the dālla.

row.basis: a sheep fallen into a pit is lifted out
row.note: Jesus assumes that an owner will take hold of and lift out a sheep fallen into a pit even on the Sabbath, a concrete recovery scene for the commentary’s animal left in an exposed place.

row.basis: found sheep carried on shoulders
row.note: After finding the lost sheep, the shepherd lays it on his shoulders with joy; this supplies the bodily return of the escaped animal that the preceding search scene alone does not state.

row.basis: owner unties ox or donkey and leads it to water
row.note: Jesus describes each person untying an ox or donkey from the stall and leading it to water, joining a known owner, a restrained domestic animal, purposeful leading, and animal provision.

row.basis: overseers shepherd God’s acquired flock
row.note: The elders must shepherd God’s flock, which God acquired, while serving as overseers. It distinguishes the true owner from delegated guides in a way that closely illuminates the commentary’s rab/mālik and leading-animal relation.

row.basis: shepherd the flock of God under oversight
row.note: The elders are told to shepherd the flock of God and exercise oversight, a specific Christian instruction about the responsibility attached to leading another’s flock.

row.basis: untrained calf asks to be turned back
row.note: Ephraim compares itself to an untrained calf and asks God to turn it back. The image gives the commentary’s tamed animal and its loss of direction a penitential human counterpart.

row.basis: shepherd moderates pace for tender flock
row.note: Jacob says tender children and nursing flocks cannot be driven hard without losing the herd. It adds a concrete criterion for a leader’s guidance: the front-moving party must accommodate the flock it leads.

row.basis: animals teach the human questioner
row.note: Job invites the sufferer to ask the animals, which will teach him. This develops the commentary’s secondary reversal in which animal life may disclose what a human who has lost the way fails to know.

row.basis: wild asses drink from God’s waters
row.note: God’s waters give drink to beasts of the field and quench the thirst of wild asses, giving the commentary’s ownerless wild-ass image a providential water-and-habitat setting.

row.basis: wild donkey wandering alone
row.note: Hosea compares political wandering to a wild donkey going alone; it supplies a biblical use of the wild-ass figure for self-directed separation rather than the secure movement of a herd.

row.basis: called by name and declared God’s own
row.note: The creator calls Israel by name and says “you are mine,” a human counterpart to the commentary’s brand that makes an animal’s belonging and owner recognizable.

row.basis: working ox must not be muzzled
row.note: The law preserves the feeding claim of an ox while it works, adding an ethical limit to treating the commentary’s tamed, useful animal solely as a bearer of human benefit.

row.basis: flock-tender receives milk from the flock
row.note: Paul’s labor argument asks who tends a flock without drinking its milk. Alongside his ox citation, this turns the material benefit of a tended flock into an analogy for the guide’s rightful support.

row.basis: seal says the Lord knows those who are his
row.note: God’s firm foundation bears a seal declaring that the Lord knows those who are his, a textual counterpart to the commentary’s visible mark and the lost camel whose owner cannot be known.

row.basis: take my yoke and learn from me
row.note: Jesus’ invitation to take his yoke and learn makes animal harness a figure for guided discipleship, offering a Christian transformation of the commentary’s subdued, neck-directed animal.
